title: Ki Tisa: even the sanctuary rests (Exodus 31:12–17)
hookLine: the building work stops for Shabbat; these verses are sung on Friday night
tomorrow: Ki Tisa: show me thy glory

cards: The biggest project in the camp is about to begin: a home for God. The plans have come down from the mountain, the gold has been collected, the best artist in the camp has been named. Everyone is eager.
And the very next thing the Torah says, right after naming Bezalel, is: stop. Not forever. Every seventh day.
Even this building, holy work, puts its tools down for Shabbat. And the verses that say so are sung in synagogues on Friday night.

teach.b: The passage begins with v'shamru, and they shall keep. In the JPS 1917 translation: "Wherefore the children of Israel shall keep the sabbath, to observe the sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant."
It calls Shabbat a sign between God and Israel forever, because in six days God made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day ceased from work and rested.
The rabbis noticed where this sits: right after all the instructions for the sanctuary.

teach.h: THE BUILDING DOESN'T PUSH SHABBAT ASIDE.
teach.b: Rashi says the point is plain: however eager you are to build, the building does not push Shabbat aside. The Talmud goes further.

When the rabbis listed the kinds of work forbidden on Shabbat, thirty-nine of them, they drew the list from the work of building the sanctuary: sowing, weaving, writing, building, kindling, and the rest.
The labors that made a home for God are exactly the labors that stop on God's day. One more word.

teach.h: VAYINAFASH: AND HE CAUGHT HIS BREATH.
teach.b: When the verse says God rested, the Hebrew is vayinafash, and Rashi hears in it nefesh, soul or breath. He reads it as catching one's breath, getting one's soul back.
Even the Creator, in the Torah's picture, pauses to breathe. V'shamru is sung in the Friday evening service, and in some communities it is said again before the Shabbat morning kiddush over wine.

how: V'shamru (Exodus 31:16–17) is sung in the Friday evening service, and in some communities it is also recited before the kiddush on Shabbat morning.

and they shall keep: the verses about keeping Shabbat

games.q: you're on Bezalel's crew. the sanctuary is half built, everyone's inspired, and Friday afternoon is fading. what does the Torah say?
o: finish it: holy work outranks the day of rest.
put the tools down: the building rests on Shabbat too.
games.why: the Shabbat command sits right after the sanctuary plans. Rashi: however eager you are, the building does not push Shabbat aside.

practice: Think of the thing you're building right now, the one that feels too important to stop, and picture setting its tools down for a whole day.
Notice what comes, relief, worry, guilt, and breathe out slowly, the way vayinafash pictures it. If you keep Shabbat, picture this week's; if not, picture a few hours.
